content.summary_of_the_paper: The manuscript proposed a neural architecture search (NAS) algorithm for 2D image classification and natural language processing. The proposed algorithm introduces a new accuracy predictor which can be computed efficiently. And the computation of the predictor relies on two constant weights of the entire search space. The difference in the output from the two sets of weights is adopted to reflect the accuracy of the final model. Moreover, the experimental results validate the proposed algorithm with public datasets of 2D image classification and natural language processing. The established NAS search space, NAS-Bench, is used in the experiments.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
<Strength>

•	The paper is well-organized and well-written.

•	The experimental results supports the claims made in the manuscripts.

•	The submitted content is related to the application of neural architecture search in computer vision and natural language processing, which is highly relevant to the ICLR audience.

•	The novelty of the proposed algorithm is good.

<Weakness>

•	The proposed algorithm may not be sound. Because the NAS results are fully relied on randomly generated model weights. The robustness of the proposed algorithm is questionable.

•	Discussion or ablation studies are not sufficient (see below).

<Comments>

1.	Does the weight initialization algorithm matter for the final performance?

2.	Is it possible to have more one pair of constant weights with averaged epsilon value and further improve the robustness of the proposed predictor?

3.	Does the actual training recipe matter for the predictor outcome?

4.	How likely to combine some of zero-cost metrics in Table 3 for better predictor performance?

5.	Does train accuracy in Figure 1 mean accuracy of training set, validation set, or testing set?

6.	Does the predictor work better for models with more parameters or models with fewer parameters?

7.	Does the predicted epsilon correlate with the accuracy/ranking in a higher order? For instance, does large epsilon value gap mean large accuracy/rank gap?

8.	Typo: Page 6, Section 3.1.2, “… on NAS-Bench-201, too…” => “… on NAS-Bench-101, too…”.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The manuscript is of moderate quality, with good clarity and good novelties.
content.summary_of_the_review: The manuscript presented an interesting study of the proposed NAS algorithm. My only concern is about the robustness of the proposed algorithm, especially on a new search space or dataset. Because the NAS results are fully relied on randomly generated model weights.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a simple zero-cost proxy for neural architecture search, which involves evaluating the network only twice using fixed weight values on a single random batch of data. They present experiments on NAS benchmarks which show strong or comparable performance compared to other zero-cost NAS algorithms in the sense of correlation metrics.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strong:

* I am not familiar with the field, but it looks like a fairly extensive literature review of existing work in zero-cost NAS.
* Simple, easy to implement baselines can be very important contributions.
* Strong results in terms of correlation compared to the baselines, but I have some questions about this methodology.
* I appreciate the study of setting epsilon. It would be nice if there was a better rule of thumb for setting these based on matrix norms, as discussed below.

Weak:

* The method would benefit greatly from more theoretical exploration, which might also guide some interesting toy experiments. Setting all the weights equal to one thing is picking a very degenerate class of matrices with a one dimensional column space spanned by the \One vector. With a short distance between the two probe points, you are taking a directional derivative here. With a long distance, you are doing something like a “random” directional check for lipschitzness. This suggests a lot of related methods using other matrices with scales picked according to the literature on weight initialization, such as [2106.10165 The Principles of Deep Learning Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.10165).  Exploring these would tell us a lot more about when this method will or won’t work, as well as connecting it better to the literature. The idea of introducing more randomness is not necessarily a problem since you are already using a random mini batch of data.

* The strong results in Table 1 are nice, but the fact that it was used as a development set means there is not an apples-to-apples comparison in the table. It is also a bit suspicious that mostly the whole state of the field as represented in that table works worse than randomly picking, when it comes to the top 10%? How many of these papers and methods were peer-reviewed? When the dataset was switched to 101, the results were significantly worse. I think for these results to be really convincing, you would want to replicate some of these experiments using the same development set for every method to pick applicable hyperparameters, even if that meant reimplementing some of the old methods for your baselines.

* The experiments in 3.3 shows epsilon metric works slightly better than random search, but could you not compare it against some other zero-cost heuristics? Many of them should be fairly straightforward to implement.

Nits / Suggestions:

* The epsilon metric probably doesn’t apply very well to experiments with the NLP architectures because of weight explosion? Another nit, is that the distinction between recurrent and feedforward doesn’t really exist with the epsilon metric, because you turn every network into a recurrent network by tying all the weights.

* The fact that the performance of such a basic rule is so strong suggests some limitations in the underlying evaluation methodology  / datasets, it might be worth talking about that in the paper.  Reminds me of other “easy baseline” papers like [1606.08390 Revisiting Visual Question Answering Baselines](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.08390) and https://nips2018vigil.github.io/static/papers/accepted/14.pdf

* You write “It makes sense to set the first weight always greater than the second one” but table 4 shows the opposite. 

* In table 4 the min and max weights are the same for PTB. This should give 0 score to everything?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Writing quality and clarity is fine, the method seems original. There are concerns as to the experimental methodology, but the results should be reproducible given the IDs of the minibatch elements used for each dataset.
content.summary_of_the_review: Not quite at the bar for ICLR. Not enough theoretical investigation, and not convincing enough / thorough enough experiments. I would like to see more characterization of what this method actually does in terms of things like Lipschitzness, and/or more thorough apples-to-apples experimental comparison to other methods using proper development set methodology and reimplementation of some baselines.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work presents a novel zero-cost NAS scoring metric epsilon. It measures how different are the outputs of neural networks depending on the value of the constant shared weight used at initialization. It shows a positive correlation between the score and the performance of the neural networks. The metric is used to score architectures in NAS. Experiments compared to other zero-shot NAS metrics on three benchmark datasets demonstrate the advantage of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The proposed metric is novel and motivated by previous works on zero-shot NAS.
2. The method is easy to follow and apply.
3. Further analysis on the hyper-parameter and weight initialization are insightful. 

Weaknesses:
1. In Table 3, it seems that on NAS-Bench-NLP, the proposed metric still performs not well, though better than others measured. There are only 3 architectures in Top-10%/top-10% and Top-64/top-5%. The Kendall is not measured for other methods/metrics to compare with. Can it be really to NLP architectures?
2. In table 4, why the optimal weights are identical for NAS-Bench-NLP?
3. The weight still requires manually set for different search space (also noted by the authors)
4. In table 1, what do the second column in Top-10%/top-10% mean? Are there missing brackets?
5. Why not compare to other NAS/Zero-shot NAS methods on the performance of discovered architectures? E.g. [1] and [2]
6. The underline principal of the relationship between proposed metric and the performance is still not clearly stated. This should be elaborated more. Say, why constant weight initialization works? Why is it better than multiple random initializations to reduce variance?

Some typos:
  - Page 8, 'Tables 8,8,9'
  - Page 9, 'It is reflects'
  - Page 7, 'with and without warm-up Then', missing dot.
  - Page 5, 'Top-64/top-10%'

References:
[1] Joe Mellor, Jack Turner, Amos Storkey, and Elliot J Crowley. Neural architecture search without training. In International Conference on Machine Learning, 2021.
[2] Ming Lin, Pichao Wang, Zhenhong Sun, Hesen Chen, Xiuyu Sun, Qi Qian, Hao Li, and Rong Jin. Zen-nas: A zero-shot nas for high-performance image recognition. In International Conference on Computer Vision, 2021.
content.summary_of_the_review: Though there exist some weaknesses, I think the work is of good quality with novel method and experiments. However, there still remains some parts to be clarified.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a zero-cost(training-free) evaluation metric for scoring hundreds of candidate models in the Neural Architecture Search (NAS). The zero-cost NAS method is based on two constant shared weights initializations. The empirical results are sound to validate the efficiency of the proposed metric.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 
1. Zero-shot NAS is a real and interesting problem with limited existing works.
2. The paper has provided extensive evaluations of different metrics and datasets. The empirical results are sound to validate the efficiency of the proposed metric. 

Weakness
1. My major concern is the novelty of this paper. This work is an empirical advancement and the theoretical novelty is limited.
2. The theoretical insights from the proposed metric are a bit unclear. How to quantify is the relationship between you epsilon and ranking consistency? How does the epsilon preserve ranking consistency between the rankings produced by your epsilon when compared with the rankings produced by final trained accuracy?
3. The authors should properly proofread the entire paper because there are several typos. 
4. There are several missing baselines for comparison in the experiment setup and results, such as baselines shown as follows.
-  Joe Mellor, Jack Turner, Amos Storkey, and Elliot J Crowley. Neural architecture search without training. In International Conference on Machine Learning, 2021.
- Wuyang Chen, Xinyu Gong, and Zhangyang Wang. Neural architecture search on imagenet in four gpu hours: A theoretically inspired perspective. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2021. 
- Ming Lin, Pichao Wang, Zhenhong Sun, Hesen Chen, Xiuyu Sun, Qi Qian, Hao Li, and Rong Jin. Zen-nas: A zero-shot nas for high-performance image recognition. In International Conference on Computer Vision, 2021.
- Zhihao Zhang and Zhihao Jia. Gradsign: Model performance inference with theoretical insights. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2022.

content.title: Light and Accurate: Neural Architecture Search via Two Constant Shared Weights Initialisations
content.TL;DR: Zero-cost neural architecture search with two forward passes: no gradients, no labels, any architecture type, high accuracy.
content.abstract: In recent years, zero-cost proxies are gaining grounds in the field of neural architecture search (NAS). These methods allow to find the optimal neural network for a given task faster and with lesser computational load than conventional NAS methods. Equally important is the fact that they also shed some light on the internal workings of neural architectures. In this paper we present a zero-cost metric that is highly correlated with the train accuracy across the NAS-Bench-101, NAS-Bench-201 and NAS-Bench-NLP benchmark datasets. Architectures are initialised with two distinct constant shared weights, one at a time. Then, a fixed random mini-batch of data is passed forward through each initialisation. We observe that the dispersion of the outputs between two initialisations is positively correlated with trained accuracy. The correlation further improves when the dispersion is normalised by the average output magnitude. Our metric does not require gradients computation and true labels. It thus unbinds NAS procedure from training hyperparameters, loss metric and human-labelled data. Our method is easy to integrate within existing NAS algorithms and takes a fraction of second to evaluate a single network.
